newsitem.title: USA: YEARENDER - Some US inflation pressure seen in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEARENDER - Some US inflation pressure seen in 1997.

text.p: U.S. inflation has bottomed and the pace of price increases could pick up moderately in 1997, opening the window for a slightly more restrictive Federal Reserve monetary policy, economists told Reuters.

"Inflation overall has bottomed out for the business cycle and though food and energy prices may increase more moderately next year, the core rate should show some acceleration," said Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Banks Inc.
Last week the Labor Department reported that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) was up 3.3 percent from a year ago.
The core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy items, was up 2.6 percent year-over-year, it said.

"Labor market tightness and a strong economy will result in faster increases in prices of services," reasoned Reaser. "Also a worldwide economic recovery will likely put more upward pressure on commodity prices," she said.

Reaser said she does not expect inflation to become a great problem in 1997, only that it will likely pose a greater risk than it did in 1995 or 1996. To counter that risk, the Fed "might take some action in the first part of 1997 to forestall greater price pressures," she said.
Volatility that does not translate into real, permanent inflation could be one hallmark of the 1997 price picture, said Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd.

"Just because a price goes up does not mean that you have inflation," said Kahan. "The more relevant question is what happens when the price of tomatoes goes to $5.00 a pound from $1.00? If people buy a cheaper vegetable instead, the higher tomato prices are not inflationary."
Actual inflation will occur only if the government increases spending or the central bank boosts the money supply, thus validating higher prices, Kahan said.
But Kahan said neither scenario is likely, since major industrialized nations and emerging market countries are all enlisting as soldiers in the anti-inflation camp.
He predicted prices would be volatile in 1997, with sharp declines or sharp increases due to factors such as the weather.

"Producers of basic raw materials have reduced inventories to very, very low levels," he said. "That means that individual commodities are more susceptible to shocks. A bumper crop will cause prices to decline a lot. A drought or an early frost will cause prices to go higher."

Even though a sharp price increase of a particular commodity might grab a headline, its impact on the total inflation profile will be limited, said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

"The only place inflation can come from is wage pressures because labor costs are 70 percent of the cost of producting goods and services," said Williams. "Higher labor costs are both necessary and sufficient to cause any lasting inflation pressure. A commodity price increase wouldn't amount to a hill of beans."

Williams predicted inflation would begin to edge up in 1997, "reflecting the fact that the economy is growing at a pace just a little above its long-run, non-inflationary speed limit of two percent." With GDP growing at a 2.5 percent rate, the Fed will need to raise interest rates modestly in 1997, he said.
"The Fed funds rate, now at 5-1/4 percent, is likely to go to 5-1/2 percent or 5-3/4 percent," Williams predicted.
Irwin Kellner, chief economist at Chase Manhattan's Regional Bank, took a different view.
"Since the CPI is believed to overstate inflation by one percentage point, that leaves us with virtual price stability for most of 1997," said Kellner, forecasting 1997 inflation of 2.3 percent.
That implies the Fed's next monetary policy move will be to cut interest rates, not raise them, he said.
"My guess is that would occur in the first four months of 1997," said Kellner.
Marty Regalia, chief economist at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, holds a similar opinion regarding 1997 inflation.
"We just don't see anything out there at this point that is a significant inflation factor," he said.
International competitive pressures are working to keep prices down, said Regalia.
"Firms don't have the ability to pass on price increases as easily as they once could," he said.

Several factors will keep the economy running below its full growth potential, Regalia said. These include restrained government spending, "very limited" business investment in infrastructure like new plants, a less robust housing sector and relatively modest consumer spending.
"We see lackluster growth that won't give rise to inflationary pressures," Regalia said.
